title: Level 3 Capstone — My English Voice
overview: The last unit of the course, and the last verb form in it. Say how long you had been doing something before a turning point, and put all four perfect forms on one timeline. Then do the thing this level has been building towards: name your own gap precisely, set one priority, and write a plan you can actually follow.
learningPath: The lesson: listen first, then read it back.
Words: four groups, 20 words. Listen and say each one.
Patterns: 5 cards. Read the one done for you before you try.
Reading: an account of a plateau, a page about how languages are learned, and a learner's own plan.
Speaking: tap the mic, say it, listen back.
Writing: four tasks, each with a model.
Practice and the check: 7 exercises, then 12 questions.
functions: Say how long you had been doing something before a turning point
Choose the right perfect form for what you are actually saying
Describe your own progress and difficulties accurately
Name a gap precisely enough to practise it
Set one priority and say what you are setting aside
Build a habit out of a time and a place
Decide what to learn next without being told
lectureScript:
This is the last unit of the course, and it has two jobs.
The first is one new form, which is the last one you will meet here.
The second is the reason the course can stop at B1 without leaving you stranded.

The form first. The past perfect continuous.
Had, been, and an -ing form. I had been studying for two years before I could follow a meeting.
Unit 11 gave you its present twin: I have been working here for six years, reaching up to now.
This one reaches up to a point in the PAST and stops there.
It does the same job its twin does, moved back. It explains what follows it.
The road was wet: it had been raining. He was exhausted: he had been driving since five.
And the error is the one you have met four times now. Do not drop the been.
It is three pieces: had, been, and the -ing.

The second card is only possible in this unit, because the fourth form did not exist until now.
You have all four perfects, and two questions choose between them.
First: does it reach up to now, or up to a point in the past? Now takes have. The past takes had.
Second: is the point the result, or the activity? The result takes the simple. The activity takes been plus -ing.
And one rule overrides both. A number forces the simple, every time.
I have written three reports. Never I have been writing three reports.

The third and fourth cards gather things this level built in other places.
The two-word verbs of learning: keep up with, catch up on, fall behind, get through, take in, brush up on, pick up, work on.
Test each one with a pronoun, as Unit 12 taught. That still tells you whether it splits.
And there is one pair worth separating, because most learners get it wrong about themselves.
Pick up is learning by exposure, without trying. Work on is deliberate practice.
Vocabulary and idiom get picked up. The conditionals do not.
The fourth card brings together the prepositions from Unit 1 and Unit 8 and turns them on your own progress.
Good AT listening. A gap IN my listening. Working ON my listening.
One idea, three prepositions, because an adjective, a noun and a verb each bring their own. The meaning never predicts it.
And improve takes nothing at all. I want to improve my listening.

Now the last card, and it is not grammar.
The reading in this unit is by somebody who spent a year not improving, and it is the most useful year they describe.
They had been reading articles every day and looking up what they did not know. It had worked, and then it stopped working.
So they did more of it, and nothing changed.
What they eventually worked out is that reading was already their strongest thing. They had been getting better at what they were already good at.
That is what a plateau usually is. Not too little effort. Practice that has stopped stretching you.
And the fix began with something very small.
They had been saying my listening is bad. That is not a gap. It is a mood.
What they could actually not do was follow three people talking at once with no topic named.
Once you can say it that precisely, the practice designs itself. Recordings with several speakers.
So the shape of a plan you can actually follow is five steps.
Name the gap precisely enough that somebody else could design the practice.
Choose one priority, not five. A list of ten priorities is a list of none.
Turn it into a habit with a time and a place, not an amount. An hour a day depends on finding an hour; the bus comes anyway.
Fix a benchmark and never change it, because a benchmark that moves cannot show you anything.
And expect a plateau, and know what it is telling you.

One last thing, about where this course ends.
It ends at B1, and that is on purpose. B1 is roughly where a language stops being a subject and starts being something you use.
You can deal with most situations that arise at work or travelling. You can build an argument, judge a source, write connected text, and read something you were not given.
What comes after that is not another course. It is exposure you choose, use you make yourself do, and gaps you name on your own.
That is what autonomy means, and it is what the last card is for.
The word in this unit's vocabulary that matters most is not fluency or accuracy. It is voice.
Accuracy you can be taught. Fluency comes with use. A voice arrives when you stop translating what somebody else would say, and say what you mean.
That one nobody can give you, and you do not need a course for it.
Start with the words. Say each one aloud before you move on.

words.meaning: The way you sound in a language: your own manner of saying things.
words.example: It took three years before I had a voice in English.
practice: A voice is more than accuracy: it is how you sound like yourself.
Having a voice means the language stops being borrowed.
It also means the sound you make, and the active or passive voice.
Nobody gives you a voice. It arrives from use.
words.tutor: Describe your own voice in English. Ask the tutor what it sounds like.

words.meaning: A phrase whose meaning is not in its words; or the natural way a language is used.
words.example: The grammar was right and the idiom was not.
practice: An idiom is a fixed phrase, from Unit 4.
Idiom also means the natural usage of a language, as a whole.
Idiomatic means sounding like a native speaker.
Correct and idiomatic are two different achievements.
words.tutor: Describe something idiomatic. Ask the tutor how it differs from correct.

words.meaning: The ability to keep going without stopping to search.
words.example: Fluency is about not stopping, not about being right.
practice: Fluency is speed and continuity.
It is measured against hesitation, not against error.
Its adjective is fluent.
You can be fluent and inaccurate, and accurate and halting.
words.tutor: Describe your fluency. Ask the tutor what it is measured against.

words.meaning: The ability to get the forms right.
words.example: Accuracy improved long before fluency did.
practice: Accuracy is correctness of form.
It is the other half of the pair with fluency.
Its adjective is accurate.
Working on one often costs the other, temporarily.
words.tutor: Describe your accuracy. Ask the tutor how it trades against fluency.

words.meaning: Sounding like yourself rather than like a textbook.
words.example: Authenticity is the last thing to arrive.
practice: Authenticity is saying what you actually mean.
It comes after accuracy and after fluency, usually.
Its adjective is authentic.
A phrase can be correct, fluent and still not yours.
words.tutor: Describe authenticity. Ask the tutor where it sits against the other two.

words.meaning: The thing you will work on before the others.
words.example: My priority is listening, not vocabulary.
practice: A priority is what comes first, so there can only be one or two.
Priority takes over: a priority over the others.
Its verb is prioritise.
A list of ten priorities is a list of none.
words.tutor: Name one priority. Ask the tutor whether it was really one.

words.meaning: Something you cannot yet do that you need to.
words.example: The gap is not vocabulary; it is speed.
practice: Gap takes in: a gap in my listening.
A gap is specific; a weakness is vague.
Naming a gap precisely is most of the work of fixing it.
It is also the space between two things.
words.tutor: Name a gap precisely. Ask the tutor whether it was specific enough.

words.meaning: A period when you stop improving despite continuing.
words.example: I was on a plateau for about a year.
practice: A plateau is flat: effort continues and progress does not.
It is pronounced PLAT-oh.
Plateaus usually mean the practice has stopped stretching you.
It is also a verb: progress plateaued.
words.starter: I was on a plateau in …
words.tutor: Describe a plateau. Ask the tutor what usually causes one.

words.meaning: Done on purpose, with attention, rather than by habit.
words.example: Deliberate practice is uncomfortable, which is how you know it is working.
practice: Deliberate practice targets what you cannot do yet.
Comfortable practice repeats what you can.
As a verb it is said differently: de-LIB-er-ate, to think carefully.
The adjective is de-LIB-er-ut.
words.starter: Deliberate practice for me would mean …
words.tutor: Describe deliberate practice. Ask the tutor how it differs from ordinary practice.

words.meaning: A plan of what will be learned, in what order.
words.example: I wrote my own syllabus for the first time this year.
practice: A syllabus is a plan with an order in it.
Its plural is syllabuses, or syllabi.
A syllabus you wrote yourself is the point of this unit.
A list of topics is not a syllabus until it has an order.
words.starter: My syllabus for the next … is …
words.tutor: Describe a syllabus. Ask the tutor what makes it more than a list.

words.meaning: Something you do regularly without deciding to each time.
words.example: The habit matters more than the hour.
practice: A habit runs without a decision, which is its value.
Habit takes of: the habit of reading at night.
Small and daily beats large and occasional.
Its adjective is habitual.
words.tutor: Describe a habit. Ask the tutor why it beats an occasional effort.

words.meaning: Doing something regularly over a long period.
words.example: Consistency beat intensity every time.
practice: Consistency is about frequency, not about amount.
Its adjective is consistent, which takes with.
Twenty minutes daily outlasts three hours on a Sunday.
It is the single best predictor of progress.
words.tutor: Describe consistency. Ask the tutor how it differs from intensity.

words.meaning: The ease that comes from having kept going.
words.example: I lost momentum in August and it took a month to get back.
practice: Momentum builds, and it is lost faster than it is built.
It is uncountable.
Losing momentum costs more than the days you missed.
It is pronounced mo-MEN-tum.
words.tutor: Describe losing momentum. Ask the tutor what it actually costs.

words.meaning: Surrounding yourself with the language.
words.example: Immersion helps only if you understand most of what you hear.
practice: Immersion means being in the language, not just near it.
Its verb is immerse, which takes in.
Immersion without comprehension is only noise.
It is one of the most misunderstood words in language learning.
words.tutor: Describe immersion. Ask the tutor when it does not work.

words.meaning: Contact with the language, in quantity.
words.example: Exposure is necessary and it is not sufficient.
practice: Exposure takes to: exposure to the language.
Its verb is expose.
Exposure builds recognition; production needs use.
Hearing a word twenty times is not the same as using it once.
words.tutor: Describe your exposure. Ask the tutor what it does and does not build.

words.meaning: The level you have reached, measured against a standard.
words.example: Proficiency is measured; competence is what you can do.
practice: Proficiency takes in: proficiency in English.
It is usually stated against a scale such as the CEFR.
Its adjective is proficient, which also takes in.
A proficiency level is a claim somebody else can check.
words.tutor: State a proficiency level. Ask the tutor what scale it refers to.

words.meaning: What you can actually do with the language.
words.example: My competence is wider than my proficiency level suggests.
practice: Competence is ability; proficiency is the measured level.
Competence takes in.
Its adjective is competent.
The two often differ, in both directions.
words.tutor: Describe your competence. Ask the tutor how it differs from proficiency.

words.meaning: A fixed point you measure progress against.
words.example: I use the same recording every six months as a benchmark.
practice: A benchmark must stay the same to be useful.
It is also a verb: to benchmark against something.
Changing the benchmark hides the progress.
It is one word.
words.tutor: Describe a benchmark. Ask the tutor why it must stay the same.

words.meaning: The ability to direct your own learning.
words.example: Autonomy is what this level was building towards.
practice: Autonomy means choosing what to learn and how.
Its adjective is autonomous.
It is the point at which a course becomes optional.
It is pronounced aw-TON-o-mee.
words.tutor: Describe autonomy. Ask the tutor what it makes optional.

words.meaning: The move from one stage to the next.
words.example: The transition from learning to using took a year.
practice: Transition takes from and to.
Its verb is transition, or make a transition.
A transition is gradual: nothing changes on one day.
Its adjective is transitional.
words.tutor: Describe a transition. Ask the tutor to check the prepositions.

grammar.title: I had been studying for two years
grammar.explanation:
One new form, and it is the last in the course.
Unit 11 gave you the present perfect continuous: I have been working here for
six years, reaching up to now.
This is its past twin. It reaches up to a point IN THE PAST, and stops there.
grammar.rule:
had + BEEN + the -ing form. It never changes for the person.

I had been studying for two years before I could follow a meeting.
She had been waiting an hour when they finally rang.
They had been working short all week, which is why nobody checked.

What it adds over the plain past perfect:
I had studied for two years.      the fact, and it was finished
I had been studying for two years. the activity, running up to that moment

IT OFTEN EXPLAINS the event that follows it:
The road was wet: it had been raining.
He was exhausted: he had been driving since five.
That is the same job its present twin does, moved back.

State verbs refuse it, as they refuse every continuous:
NOT: I had been knowing her for years.
YES: I had known her for years.
grammar.workedExample:
One done, step by step.
You studied for two years, and then you could follow a meeting. Write it.
1. Two past points: the studying, and the moment you could follow a meeting.
2. The studying ran UP TO that moment, so it is the earlier one, and continuous.
3. had been studying.
Answer: I had been studying for two years before I could follow a meeting.
I had studied for two years would state it as a finished fact rather than as
the stretch that led up to the change.
grammar.mistake:
It is the been that goes missing, exactly as in the passive and the perfect.
No: I had studying for two years.
Yes: I had been studying for two years.
Three pieces: had, been, and the -ing form.
grammar.tip: had been + -ing. It runs up to a past moment and explains it.
grammar.practice:
Write the past perfect continuous.
1. I ___ (study) for two years before I could follow a meeting.
2. She ___ (wait) an hour when they rang.
3. They ___ (work) short all week, which is why nobody checked.
4. The road was wet: it ___ (rain).
5. He was exhausted: he ___ (drive) since five.
Now choose the better form and say why.
6. I (had studied / had been studying) for two years, and then I stopped.
7. I (had known / had been knowing) her for years.
grammar.answers:
1. had been studying  2. had been waiting  3. had been working
4. had been raining  5. had been driving
6. had studied. It is a finished fact, not a stretch leading to something.
7. had known. know is a state verb and takes no continuous.
6 or more right: good.

grammar.title: Four perfect forms, one timeline
grammar.explanation:
You now have all four, and this is the first unit in which that is true.
Putting them side by side is what a capstone is for: each one answers a
different question, and knowing which question you are answering is the
whole of the choice.
grammar.rule:
REACHING UP TO NOW:
I have studied for two years.        the fact, and how much
I have been studying for two years.  the activity, and how long

REACHING UP TO A POINT IN THE PAST:
I had studied for two years.         the fact, before that moment
I had been studying for two years.   the activity, running up to that moment

THE TWO QUESTIONS THAT DECIDE IT:
1. Does it reach up to NOW, or up to a point in the PAST?
   Now takes have. The past takes had.
2. Is the point the RESULT, or the ACTIVITY?
   The result takes the simple. The activity takes been plus -ing.

AND THE RULE THAT OVERRIDES BOTH:
A number forces the simple, in all four.
I have written three reports.  I had written three reports.
Never I have been writing three reports.

Set out with a date, the four are unmistakable:
By 2019 I had been studying for two years.
By now I have been studying for six.
grammar.workedExample:
One done, step by step.
Choose the form: By 2019 I ___ for two years, and I still study now.
1. Does the two years reach up to now, or up to 2019? Up to 2019.
2. So it takes had, not have.
3. Is the point the result or the stretch? The stretch.
4. So been plus -ing.
Answer: By 2019 I had been studying for two years.
The fact that you still study now is a separate sentence, in the present perfect.
grammar.mistake:
Learners choose have where the sentence names a past point.
No: By 2019 I have been studying for two years.
Yes: By 2019 I had been studying for two years.
If there is a past point in the sentence, the perfect has to be a past one.
grammar.tip: Two questions: up to when, and result or activity. A number overrides both.
grammar.practice:
Choose one of the four perfect forms.
1. By 2019 I ___ (study) for two years. (the stretch, up to 2019)
2. I ___ (study) for six years now. (the stretch, up to now)
3. I ___ (write) three reports this week. (a number, up to now)
4. By March I ___ (write) three of them. (a number, up to March)
5. She ___ (wait) an hour when they rang. (the stretch, up to that moment)
6. He ___ (know) her for years before he asked. (a state verb)
Now answer.
7. What are the two questions that decide between all four?
grammar.answers:
1. had been studying  2. have been studying  3. have written
4. had written  5. had been waiting  6. had known
7. Does it reach up to now or to a past point? And is the point the result or
   the activity? A number overrides the second and forces the simple.
6 or more right: good.

grammar.title: Keep up with, catch up on, fall behind
grammar.explanation:
The last set of two-word verbs in the course, and they are the ones you need
to talk about your own learning.
Test each with a pronoun, as Unit 12 taught: that still tells you the kind.
grammar.rule:
keep up with   = stay level with something that keeps moving
  I could not keep up with the reading.
catch up on    = do what you missed
  I spent August catching up on it.
fall behind    = drop below where you should be
  I fell behind in the second term.
get through    = finish a quantity of something
  I got through four books that winter.
take in        = understand and retain
  I could hear it but I was not taking it in.
brush up on    = improve something you once knew
  I need to brush up on the conditionals.
pick up        = learn without studying
  I picked most of that up from work.
work on        = practise deliberately
  I am working on my listening.

THE PAIR TO KEEP APART:
pick up  = learned by exposure, without trying
work on  = learned by deliberate practice
Most learners overestimate how much they will pick up, which is why the next
card matters.
grammar.workedExample:
One done, step by step.
You heard the language constantly but did not understand much. Which verb?
1. Did you hear it? Yes.
2. Did you understand and retain it? No.
3. That is exactly what take in means, in the negative.
Answer: I could hear it, but I was not taking it in.
Test the kind with a pronoun: I was not taking IT in. It splits, so it is
the separable kind from Unit 12.
grammar.mistake:
Learners say pick up for things nobody picks up.
Vocabulary and idiom are picked up. The conditionals are not.
Anything a listener will forgive is picked up. Anything they will not, you
have to work on.
grammar.tip: Test the kind with a pronoun. And keep pick up apart from work on.
grammar.practice:
Complete each one with a verb from the card.
1. I could not ___ ___ ___ the reading; it was too fast.
2. I spent August ___ ___ ___ it.
3. I ___ ___ in the second term.
4. I ___ ___ four books that winter.
5. I could hear it but I was not ___ it ___ .
6. I need to ___ ___ ___ the conditionals.
7. I ___ most of that ___ from work, without studying.
8. I am ___ ___ my listening, deliberately.
Now say which of the eight split, by testing them with a pronoun.
grammar.answers:
1. keep up with  2. catching up on  3. fell behind  4. got through
5. taking it in  6. brush up on  7. picked ... up  8. working on
Split: take in and pick up (I was not taking IT in; I picked it UP).
Do not split: keep up with, catch up on, fall behind, get through,
brush up on, work on.
7 or more right: good.

grammar.title: Good at, a gap in, working on
grammar.explanation:
The last card of grammar in this course gathers something built in three
separate places: Unit 1 gave you the preposition an adjective brings, and
Unit 8 gave you the ones nouns and verbs bring.
Here they are together, and turned on your own progress.
grammar.rule:
AFTER AN ADJECTIVE (Unit 1):
good AT listening        capable OF following a meeting
aware OF the gap         confident IN writing
reluctant TO speak       proficient IN English

AFTER A NOUN (Unit 8):
a gap IN my listening    confidence IN speaking
a difficulty WITH idiom  an improvement IN accuracy
the reason FOR the plateau  exposure TO the language

AFTER A VERB (Unit 8):
work ON listening        rely ON subtitles
struggle WITH idiom      improve (no preposition at all)
succeed IN following it  apply FOR a place

THE ONES THAT CATCH PEOPLE WRITING ABOUT THEMSELVES:
good AT, not good in.
a gap IN, not a gap of.
work ON, not work in.
proficiency IN, not proficiency of.
And improve takes NOTHING: I want to improve my listening.
grammar.workedExample:
One done, step by step.
Say that listening is where you are weakest, three ways.
1. With an adjective: good takes at. I am not very good AT listening.
2. With a noun: gap takes in. There is a gap IN my listening.
3. With a verb: work takes on. I am working ON my listening.
Answer: all three, and each uses a different preposition for the same idea.
That is why the three sources have to be learned separately: the meaning does
not predict the word.
grammar.mistake:
improve takes no preposition, and learners give it one.
No: I want to improve in my listening. / improve on my listening.
Yes: I want to improve my listening.
improve ON means to do better than an earlier attempt, which is different.
grammar.tip: Adjective, noun and verb each bring their own. The meaning never predicts it.
grammar.practice:
Write the missing preposition, or NONE.
1. I am not very good ___ listening.
2. There is a gap ___ my listening.
3. I am working ___ my listening.
4. I want to improve ___ my listening.
5. I am aware ___ the problem.
6. I rely ___ subtitles too much.
7. My proficiency ___ English is about B1.
8. I struggle ___ idiom.
9. I am confident ___ writing.
10. My exposure ___ spoken English is limited.
grammar.answers:
1. at  2. in  3. on  4. NONE  5. of  6. on
7. in  8. with  9. in  10. to
Numbers 1, 2 and 3 are the same idea with three different prepositions,
because the adjective, the noun and the verb each bring their own.
8 or more right: good.

grammar.title: Naming a gap, setting a priority
grammar.explanation:
The last card in the course is not a grammar point. It is the thing this
level has been building towards, and it is the reason the course can stop
here without leaving you stranded.
You write your own syllabus, and there is a shape that works.
grammar.rule:
STEP 1 — NAME THE GAP PRECISELY.
Weak:   my listening is bad.
Better: I lose the thread when three people talk and nobody names the topic.
A gap you can describe is a gap you can practise. One you cannot is a mood.

STEP 2 — CHOOSE ONE PRIORITY, not five.
A list of ten priorities is a list of none.
Ask which gap costs you most this year, not which is largest.

STEP 3 — TURN IT INTO A HABIT, not a project.
Twenty minutes daily outlasts three hours on a Sunday.
Name the time and the place, not the amount.

STEP 4 — FIX A BENCHMARK, and do not change it.
The same recording, or the same kind of text, every six months.
A benchmark that moves cannot show you anything.

STEP 5 — EXPECT A PLATEAU, and know what it means.
A plateau is not failure. It usually means the practice has stopped
stretching you, which is a signal to change the practice, not the effort.
grammar.workedExample:
One done, step by step.
Somebody says: my listening is bad and I want to improve it.
1. Is the gap named precisely? No. Bad is a mood, not a gap.
2. Ask when it fails. In meetings, with several speakers, with no topic given.
3. Now it is practisable: find recordings with several speakers.
4. Make it a habit with a time and a place, not an amount.
5. Fix a benchmark: the same recording every six months.
Answer: 'I lose the thread when three people talk. Twenty minutes of
multi-speaker audio on the bus each morning. Same recording every June.'
That is a syllabus. My listening is bad is not.
grammar.mistake:
The commonest failure is a plan made of amounts rather than of times.
Weak: I will do an hour a day.
Better: I will listen on the bus each morning.
The first depends on finding an hour. The second depends on the bus,
which arrives whether you feel like it or not.
grammar.tip: Name the gap so precisely that the practice is obvious. Then one priority, one habit, one benchmark.
grammar.practice:
Rewrite each vague gap as a precise one.
1. My listening is bad.
2. My grammar is weak.
3. I need more vocabulary.
4. I am not confident speaking.
Now answer.
5. Why is 'I will do an hour a day' a weaker plan than 'I will listen on the bus'?
6. What does a plateau usually mean, and what should you change?
7. Why must a benchmark stay the same?
grammar.answers:
1 to 4: yours will differ. Each should name WHEN it fails, precisely enough
that the practice is obvious. For example: 'I lose the thread when three
people talk and nobody names the topic.'
5. It depends on finding an hour. The bus arrives anyway.
6. That the practice has stopped stretching you. Change the practice, not the effort.
7. A benchmark that moves cannot show you progress.
5 or more right: good.

readings.title: The Year Nothing Happened
readings.setting: Told by somebody four years into learning
readings.passage:
I had been studying for two years before I could follow a meeting, and then I stopped improving for about a year.
That year was the most useful one, though it did not feel like it at the time.
I had been doing the same thing every day: reading articles and looking up what I did not know.
It had worked, and then it stopped working, and I assumed I was not doing enough of it.
So I did more of it, and nothing changed, which is how I learned what a plateau actually is.
It was not that I needed more effort. It was that the practice had stopped stretching me.
Reading is where I was already strongest. I had been getting better at the thing I was already good at.
What I could not do was follow three people talking at once with no topic named.
That is a precise gap, and it took me a long time to say it that precisely.
Before that I had only been able to say that my listening was bad, which is not a gap. It is a mood.
Once I could name it, the practice was obvious: recordings with several speakers, twenty minutes, on the bus.
Not an hour a day. An hour a day depends on finding an hour. The bus comes anyway.
I use the same recording every June as a benchmark, and I have never changed it, which is the only reason I can see that the year was not wasted.

readings.title: Exposure Is Necessary and Not Sufficient
readings.setting: A page about how languages are learned
readings.passage:
Two words in language learning are used almost interchangeably and mean different things.
Exposure is contact with the language, in quantity.
Immersion is being surrounded by it, usually in a place where it is spoken.
Both help, and neither works on its own, and the reason is the same for both.
Language you do not understand is noise, and noise teaches nothing however much of it you hear.
What builds a language is input you understand most but not all of, and there is a rough test.
If you can follow the sense and are missing some of the words, that material is working for you.
If you are missing the sense, it is not, however authentic it is.
There is a second limit worth knowing, and it explains a great deal of frustration.
Exposure builds recognition. Production needs use.
Hearing a word twenty times will let you recognise it. It will not let you say it at speed under pressure.
That is why people who have lived somewhere for years can still be unable to say things they understand perfectly.
The remedy is not more exposure. It is deliberate use of the specific things you cannot yet produce.
That is uncomfortable, which is the clearest sign it is the right practice.

readings.title: Learning Plan: Next Six Months
readings.setting: A plan written by a learner for themselves
readings.passage:
LEARNING PLAN — SIX MONTHS
Written: 14 June        Review: 14 December

1. Where I am
Proficiency: about B1. Competence is wider in reading than the level suggests,
and narrower in listening.
I have been studying for four years. I had been improving steadily until last
autumn, when I reached a plateau.

2. The gap
Not listening in general. I lose the thread when three or more people speak and
nobody names the topic. I can follow one speaker on any subject.

3. Priority
One only: multi-speaker listening. Vocabulary and writing are set aside until December.

4. Habit
Twenty minutes on the bus each weekday morning. Not an amount: a time and a place.

5. Benchmark
The same eight-minute recording of a four-person meeting, tested every June and December.
Unchanged since 2022.

6. What I expect to go wrong
August. I lost momentum last August and it took a month to get back.
This year: keep the habit at ten minutes rather than dropping it.

comprehension.q: How long had the writer been studying before they could follow a meeting?
comprehension.why: The past perfect continuous marks the stretch running up to that point.

comprehension.q: Why did doing more of the same not help?
comprehension.a: The practice had stopped stretching them; they were improving at what they were already good at.
comprehension.why: That is what the text says a plateau actually is.

comprehension.q: The writer says 'my listening was bad' is not a gap. What is it?
comprehension.why: A gap you can describe is one you can practise; a vague one is not.

comprehension.q: Why is 'on the bus' a better plan than 'an hour a day'?
comprehension.a: An hour a day depends on finding an hour. The bus comes anyway.
comprehension.why: The plan is tied to a time and a place rather than to an amount.

comprehension.q: What is the difference between exposure and immersion?
comprehension.a: Exposure is contact in quantity; immersion is being surrounded by the language.
comprehension.why: Both help, and neither works on its own.

comprehension.q: What is the rough test for whether material is working for you?
comprehension.a: You can follow the sense and are missing some words.
comprehension.why: If you are missing the sense, it is noise however authentic it is.

comprehension.q: Why can somebody who has lived somewhere for years still be unable to say things they understand?
comprehension.a: Exposure builds recognition; production needs use.
comprehension.why: The remedy is deliberate use, not more exposure.

comprehension.q: What single priority has the writer set, and what have they set aside?
comprehension.a: Multi-speaker listening. Vocabulary and writing are set aside until December.
comprehension.why: Section 3, and a single priority is what makes it a plan.

comprehension.q: What is the benchmark, and why does the plan say 'unchanged since 2022'?
comprehension.a: The same eight-minute four-person recording. A benchmark that moves cannot show progress.
comprehension.why: Section 5, and the date is there to prove it has not been changed.

comprehension.q: 'I had been improving steadily until last autumn.' Why not 'I had improved'?
comprehension.a: It describes a stretch running up to that point, not a finished fact.
comprehension.why: The past perfect continuous shows the activity leading to the plateau.

speaking.title: Speaking 1 — Up to a point in the past
speaking.instructions:
Say six sentences about your own learning, real or invented.
Every one must use had been plus an -ing form, running up to a past moment.
Models:
I had been studying for two years before I could follow a meeting.
I had been using subtitles until last year.
I had been avoiding the telephone for a long time before I had to use it.
Tap the mic. Say all six. Tap again and listen.
Check: does each one name a past moment that the stretch ran up to?
Did the been survive in every one?
speaking.tutor: Say your six and ask the tutor whether any of them should have been about now instead.

speaking.title: Speaking 2 — Four weak syllables in a row
speaking.instructions:
This is the longest stack of unstressed words in English, and it is the last
pronunciation point in the course.
Listen and repeat. The capitals show the stress.
I had been STUDYing     sounds like  I-d-bin STUDYing
she had been WAITing    sounds like  she-d-bin WAITing
they had been WORKing   sounds like  they-d-bin WORKing
I have been STUDYing    sounds like  I-v-bin STUDYing
Listen to the last two. The only difference is a d against a v, and it is
the difference between the past and now.
Now say these three lines.
I had been studying for two years before I could follow a meeting.
I have been studying for six years now.
They had been working short all week, which is why nobody checked.
Tap the mic. Say the three lines. Tap again and listen.
Check: can you hear your own d and v clearly enough to tell them apart?
speaking.tutor: Say lines one and two and ask the tutor which was the past one.

speaking.title: Speaking 3 — Which of the four?
speaking.instructions:
Say each one with the right perfect form.
1. By 2019 you had done two years of study. (the stretch)
2. You have done six years, up to now. (the stretch)
3. You have finished three reports this week. (a number)
4. By March you had finished three. (a number)
5. She waited an hour, and then they rang. (the stretch)
6. You knew her for years before you asked. (a state verb)
Tap the mic. Say all six. Tap again and listen.
Check: in 3 and 4, did the number force the simple?
In 6, did you avoid the continuous altogether?
speaking.tutor: Say your six and ask the tutor which two you found hardest to separate.

speaking.title: Speaking 4 — Listen: the year nothing happened
speaking.instructions:
Tap Listen. Do not read along. Listen twice.
I had been studying for two years before I could follow a meeting, and then I stopped improving for about a year.
I had been doing the same thing every day: reading articles and looking up what I did not know.
It had worked, and then it stopped working, and I assumed I was not doing enough of it.
So I did more of it, and nothing changed.
It was not that I needed more effort. It was that the practice had stopped stretching me.
Reading is where I was already strongest. I had been getting better at the thing I was already good at.
What I could not do was follow three people talking at once with no topic named.
Before that I could only say my listening was bad, which is not a gap. It is a mood.
Now answer. Tap the mic and say each answer.
1. How long before the speaker could follow a meeting?
2. What had they been doing every day?
3. Why did doing more of it not help?
4. What was the real gap?
Tap again and listen to your answers.
Check: 1 two years. 2 reading articles and looking words up.
3 the practice had stopped stretching them. 4 following three speakers with no topic named.
speaking.tutor: Retell the plateau in three sentences and ask the tutor what you would have advised.

speaking.title: Speaking 5 — Say where you are
speaking.instructions:
Answer each question aloud in one or two sentences about yourself.
Watch the preposition in every answer.
1. What are you good at?
2. Where is the gap in your English?
3. What are you working on?
4. What do you rely on too much?
5. What is your proficiency in English, and how does your competence differ?
6. What do you struggle with?
Models: I am good AT reading. There is a gap IN my listening.
I am working ON multi-speaker audio.
Tap the mic. Answer all six. Tap again and listen.
Check: did good take at, gap take in, and work take on?
If you said improve anywhere, did you give it no preposition at all?
speaking.tutor: Answer the six for the tutor and ask it to check every preposition.

speaking.title: Speaking 6 — Two minutes: your own plan
speaking.instructions:
Present your own learning plan for the next six months, for two minutes.
Cover these six, in this order:
where you are, and how long you have been studying
what you had been doing before now, and how well it worked
the gap, named so precisely that the practice is obvious
one priority, and what you are setting aside
the habit: a time and a place, not an amount
the benchmark, and when you will next test it
Use the present perfect continuous once and the past perfect continuous once.
Tap the mic. Speak for two minutes without stopping.
Tap again and listen to the whole thing.
Check: is your gap precise enough that somebody else could design the practice?
Did you name one priority, or several?
speaking.tutor: Give the tutor your plan and ask whether the gap was precise enough to act on.

writing.title: Writing 1 — Six sentences up to a past point
writing.prompt:
Write six sentences about your own learning using the past perfect continuous.
Each must run up to a named moment in the past.
Then write two more using the past perfect SIMPLE, and say why each one is simple.
writing.model:
I had been studying for two years before I could follow a meeting.
I had been using subtitles until last autumn.
I had been avoiding the telephone for a long time before I had to use it.
I had been reading the same kind of article every day until the plateau.
She had been waiting an hour when they finally rang.
They had been working short all week, which is why nobody checked.

I had finished three modules by March. (a number forces the simple)
I had known her for years before I asked. (know is a state verb)
writing.criteria:
Six past perfect continuous, each with had, been and an -ing form.
Every one names a past moment the stretch ran up to.
Two simple, with a correct reason: a number, or a state verb.
No been dropped anywhere.
writing.support: Write the past moment first, then the stretch that led up to it.
writing.extension: Rewrite one of the six as if it reached up to now, and say which word changed.

writing.title: Writing 2 — One verb, four perfect forms
writing.prompt:
Choose one verb about your learning: study, read, practise, listen or write.
Write four sentences with it, one in each perfect form, and say in brackets
which of the two questions decided each.
Then write one sentence showing a number forcing the simple.
writing.model:
I have studied for six years. (up to now; the fact)
I have been studying for six years. (up to now; the activity)
By 2019 I had studied for two years. (up to a past point; the fact)
By 2019 I had been studying for two years. (up to a past point; the activity)

I have finished three modules this year. (a number forces the simple)
writing.criteria:
All four forms present and correctly built.
Each bracket names both decisions: when it reaches, and result or activity.
The number sentence uses the simple.
The same verb used throughout.
writing.support: Draw the two questions as a grid: now against past, and result against activity. Fill in all four boxes.
writing.extension: Write the two of your four that are hardest to tell apart, and say how a reader would.

writing.title: Writing 3 — Name the gap precisely
writing.prompt:
Below are four vague statements about a learner's English.
Rewrite each one as a gap named precisely enough that the practice is obvious.
Then, for one of them, write the habit that follows, with a time and a place.
a) My listening is bad.
b) My grammar is weak.
c) I need more vocabulary.
d) I am not confident speaking.
writing.model:
a) I lose the thread when three or more people speak and nobody names the topic.
b) I can form the conditionals but I do not reach for them when I am speaking.
c) I recognise far more words than I can produce at speed under pressure.
d) I can say what I mean, but not quickly enough to interrupt anybody.

For (a): twenty minutes of multi-speaker audio on the bus each weekday morning.
Not an hour a day. The bus comes whether I feel like it or not.
writing.starter: a) I lose the thread when …
writing.criteria:
Every gap names WHEN it fails, not just what is weak.
Every gap is specific enough that somebody else could design the practice.
The habit names a time and a place rather than an amount.
No rewrite uses the words bad, weak or more.
writing.support: For each one, ask: when exactly does this fail? Answer that, and you have the gap.
writing.extension: Write the gap you would have named a year ago, and say how it has changed.

writing.title: Writing 4 — Your own learning plan
writing.prompt:
Write your own learning plan for the next six months, in six sections,
in the style of Reading 3:
Where I am, The gap, Priority, Habit, Benchmark, What I expect to go wrong.
Where I am must use the present perfect continuous and the past perfect continuous.
The gap must be precise. The priority must be ONE thing.
The habit must name a time and a place. The benchmark must be fixed and dated.
writing.model:
1. Where I am. Proficiency about B1; competence wider in reading than the level
   suggests. I have been studying for four years. I had been improving steadily
   until last autumn, when I reached a plateau.
2. The gap. Not listening in general. I lose the thread when three or more people
   speak and nobody names the topic.
3. Priority. One only: multi-speaker listening. Vocabulary and writing set aside
   until December.
4. Habit. Twenty minutes on the bus each weekday morning. A time and a place.
5. Benchmark. The same eight-minute four-person recording, every June and December.
   Unchanged since 2022.
6. What I expect to go wrong. August. Last year I lost momentum and it took a
   month to get back. This year: ten minutes rather than nothing.
writing.criteria:
Section 1 uses both continuous perfects correctly.
The gap names when it fails; the priority is a single thing.
The habit names a time and a place, not an amount.
Section 6 names a specific past failure and what will be done differently.
writing.support: Write section 2 first. Everything else follows from how precisely you name the gap.
writing.extension: Write the one sentence you would put at the top of this plan for yourself in six months.

activities.title: Practice 1 — Up to that moment
activities.instructions:
Write the past perfect continuous.
1. I ___ (study) for two years before I could follow a meeting.
2. She ___ (wait) an hour when they rang.
3. They ___ (work) short all week, which is why nobody checked.
4. The road was wet: it ___ (rain).
5. He was exhausted: he ___ (drive) since five.
6. I ___ (use) subtitles until last autumn.
Now choose the better form and say why.
7. I (had studied / had been studying) for two years, and then I stopped.
8. I (had known / had been knowing) her for years.
9. Correct: I had studying for two years.
activities.answers:
1. had been studying  2. had been waiting  3. had been working
4. had been raining  5. had been driving  6. had been using
7. had studied — a finished fact, not a stretch leading anywhere.
8. had known — know is a state verb.
9. had BEEN studying. Three pieces: had, been, -ing.
7 or more right: good.
activities.solo: Say each one aloud before writing. The been is the piece that disappears.

activities.title: Practice 2 — Which of the four?
activities.instructions:
Choose one of the four perfect forms.
1. By 2019 I ___ (study) for two years. (the stretch, up to 2019)
2. I ___ (study) for six years now. (the stretch, up to now)
3. I ___ (write) three reports this week. (a number)
4. By March I ___ (write) three of them. (a number, up to March)
5. She ___ (wait) an hour when they rang.
6. He ___ (know) her for years before he asked.
7. I ___ (read) four books this month. (a number)
8. I ___ (read) all afternoon and I am still reading.
Now answer.
9. What are the two questions that decide between all four?
activities.answers:
1. had been studying  2. have been studying  3. have written  4. had written
5. had been waiting  6. had known  7. have read  8. have been reading
9. Does it reach up to now or to a past point? And is the point the result or
   the activity? A number overrides the second and forces the simple.
7 or more right: good.
activities.solo: For each one, write NOW or PAST and then RESULT or ACTIVITY. The pair chooses the form.

activities.title: Practice 3 — The verbs of learning
activities.instructions:
Complete each one with a verb from the card.
1. I could not ___ ___ ___ the reading; it was too fast.
2. I spent August ___ ___ ___ it.
3. I ___ ___ in the second term.
4. I ___ ___ four books that winter.
5. I could hear it but I was not ___ it ___ .
6. I need to ___ ___ ___ the conditionals.
7. I ___ most of that ___ from work, without studying.
8. I am ___ ___ my listening, deliberately.
Now answer.
9. Which two of the eight split around their object?
10. What is the difference between pick up and work on?
activities.answers:
1. keep up with  2. catching up on  3. fell behind  4. got through
5. taking it in  6. brush up on  7. picked ... up  8. working on
9. take in and pick up. Test with a pronoun: I was not taking IT in.
10. pick up is learning by exposure, without trying. work on is deliberate practice.
8 or more right: good.
activities.solo: Test each one with a pronoun before you write it. That tells you whether it splits.

activities.title: Practice 4 — The preposition, one last time
activities.instructions:
Write the missing preposition, or NONE.
1. I am not very good ___ listening.
2. There is a gap ___ my listening.
3. I am working ___ my listening.
4. I want to improve ___ my listening.
5. I am aware ___ the problem.
6. I rely ___ subtitles too much.
7. My proficiency ___ English is about B1.
8. I struggle ___ idiom.
9. I am confident ___ writing.
10. My exposure ___ spoken English is limited.
11. The reason ___ the plateau was the practice.
12. I am reluctant ___ speak on the telephone.
activities.answers:
1. at  2. in  3. on  4. NONE  5. of  6. on
7. in  8. with  9. in  10. to  11. for  12. to
1, 2 and 3 are the same idea with three different prepositions, because an
adjective, a noun and a verb each bring their own.
Number 4 is improve, which takes nothing at all.
10 or more right: good.
activities.solo: Mark each gap A, N or V for adjective, noun or verb. Then recall which source it comes from.

activities.title: Practice 5 — Make the gap precise
activities.instructions:
Rewrite each vague statement as a gap you could practise.
1. My listening is bad.
2. My grammar is weak.
3. I need more vocabulary.
4. I am not confident speaking.
5. My writing is not natural.
Now answer.
6. What makes a gap precise enough to act on?
7. Why is 'I will do an hour a day' a weaker plan than 'I will listen on the bus'?
activities.answers:
Yours will differ. Each should name WHEN it fails.
1. I lose the thread when three or more people speak with no topic named.
2. I can form the conditionals but do not reach for them when speaking.
3. I recognise far more words than I can produce at speed.
4. I can say what I mean, but not quickly enough to interrupt.
5. My sentences are correct but longer than a native speaker would write.
6. Somebody else could design the practice from it, without asking you anything.
7. An hour a day depends on finding an hour. The bus comes anyway.
5 or more right: good.
activities.solo: For each one, ask when exactly it fails. Write that, and delete the original.

activities.title: Practice 6 — Exposure, or use?
activities.instructions:
For each situation, say whether the problem is a lack of exposure or a lack
of deliberate use, and what you would do.
1. You understand the news but cannot discuss it.
2. You have lived somewhere four years and still cannot say things you understand.
3. You listen to podcasts daily and follow almost none of them.
4. You know all the conditional forms and never use them in speech.
5. You read easily and lose the thread the moment three people speak.
activities.answers:
1. Use. Recognition is there; production is not. Practise saying it, not hearing more.
2. Use, almost certainly. Exposure builds recognition; production needs use.
3. Neither, exactly. The material is too hard: it is noise. Find input you follow
   most but not all of.
4. Use, and deliberate. Knowing a form is not reaching for it under pressure.
5. A precise gap, and it needs targeted exposure: multi-speaker audio specifically.
Note that only number 5 is solved by more listening, and only of one particular kind.
4 or 5 right: good.
activities.solo: For each, ask whether you can already recognise it. If yes, the problem is use.

activities.title: Practice 7 — Find it in the plan
activities.instructions:
Answer from Reading 3 only.
1. How long has the writer been studying, and when did the plateau start?
2. What exactly is the gap, and what is it NOT?
3. What has been set aside, and until when?
4. Copy the habit and say what it names instead of an amount.
5. Why does the benchmark say 'unchanged since 2022'?
6. What does section 6 do that most plans leave out?
activities.answers:
1. Four years; the plateau started last autumn.
2. Losing the thread when three or more speak with no topic named. It is NOT
   listening in general: one speaker on any subject is fine.
3. Vocabulary and writing, until December.
4. 'Twenty minutes on the bus each weekday morning.' It names a time and a place.
5. To prove the benchmark has not moved. A benchmark that changes cannot show progress.
6. It names what is expected to go wrong, and what will be done instead of stopping.
5 or 6 right: good.
activities.solo: Read the plan and mark which of the six sections your own plan is missing.

quizzes.q: I ___ for two years before I could follow a meeting.
quizzes.why: The stretch ran up to a moment in the PAST, so had rather than have. And three pieces: had, been and the -ing form.

options: I had been waiting an hour.
I had been knowing her for years.
They had been working short all week.
quizzes.a: I had been knowing her for years.
quizzes.why: know is a state verb and refuses every continuous form. I had known her for years is correct.

quizzes.q: By 2019 I ___ for two years. (the stretch, and it reaches up to 2019)
quizzes.why: A past point in the sentence forces a past perfect. have been studying would reach up to now instead.
A number counts finished things, so it forces the simple, in all four perfect forms. And this week reaches up to now.

quizzes.q: I could hear it but I was not ___ .
quizzes.why: take in means understand and retain, and it splits around a pronoun. taking in it is not possible.

quizzes.q: What is the difference between picking something up and working on it?
options: Picking up is by exposure; working on is deliberate.
Working on is only for grammar.
quizzes.a: Picking up is by exposure; working on is deliberate.
quizzes.why: Vocabulary and idiom are picked up. Anything a listener will not forgive, you have to work on.

quizzes.q: There is a gap ___ my listening.
quizzes.why: gap takes in. The adjective good takes at, and the verb work takes on: three prepositions for one idea.

quizzes.q: I want to improve ___ my listening.
quizzes.why: improve takes a direct object with no preposition. improve ON means to do better than an earlier attempt, which is different.

quizzes.q: Which is a gap you could act on?
options: I lose the thread when three people speak and nobody names the topic.
I need to improve my English.
quizzes.a: I lose the thread when three people speak and nobody names the topic.
quizzes.why: It names WHEN it fails, so somebody else could design the practice from it. The others are moods rather than gaps.

quizzes.q: What does a plateau usually mean?
options: You are not working hard enough.
The practice has stopped stretching you.
quizzes.a: The practice has stopped stretching you.
quizzes.why: It is a signal to change the practice, not to increase the effort. Doing more of what already worked is the commonest response and the wrong one.

quizzes.q: Why is 'I will listen on the bus' a better plan than 'I will do an hour a day'?
options: It names a time and a place rather than an amount.
quizzes.a: It names a time and a place rather than an amount.
quizzes.why: An hour a day depends on finding an hour. The bus comes whether you feel like it or not.

quizzes.q: Somebody has lived abroad four years and still cannot say things they understand. What do they need?
options: Deliberate use of what they cannot yet produce
quizzes.a: Deliberate use of what they cannot yet produce
quizzes.why: Exposure builds recognition; production needs use. More of what built the recognition will not build the production.

teacherNotes.note: The past perfect continuous (9Ug.08) is the last new verb form in the course. Card 2 is the first time all four perfect forms can be set side by side, because the fourth did not exist before this unit. Cards 3 and 4 are pure consolidation of 9Ug.11 and 9Uv.01, gathering material from L2 U15, Unit 1, Unit 8 and Unit 12.
This unit has twenty words in four groups rather than twenty-nine in five, as the plan allocates. That is the capstone allowance and is not an omission.

Card 5 is the point of the unit and of the level. It carries no grammar and it is what makes stopping at B1 defensible: a learner who can name a gap precisely, set one priority and fix a benchmark does not need another course. If time is short, teach card 5 properly and let card 3 go.

The dropped been has now appeared in the passive (Unit 10), the perfect passive (Unit 10 and 18), the present perfect continuous (Unit 11) and here. Name the pattern across all four rather than treating it as new: every stacked form loses its middle piece.

'A number forces the simple' was taught in Unit 11 for the present perfect. Learners apply it there and not here. Practice 2 items 3 and 4 are the same number in two different time frames for that reason.

Reading 1 describes a year of no visible progress, and the unit treats that as normal and informative rather than as failure. Learners arriving at the end of a course often expect to have finished; the lecture says explicitly what B1 is and is not, and what comes after it. Do not let the unit be taught as a completion.

Writing 4 is the assignment in miniature and the real assessment: a plan for the learner's own next six months. It is marked on whether the gap is precise enough that somebody else could design the practice from it, which is the only criterion that predicts whether the plan will be followed.

selfAssessment.statement: I can say how long I had been doing something before a turning point.
I never drop the been from had been or have been.
I can choose between all four perfect forms.
I know that a number forces the simple form.
I can say good at, a gap in and working on, each with its own preposition.
I know the difference between picking something up and working on it.
I can name a gap precisely enough that the practice is obvious.
I have one priority, one habit and one benchmark, and I know what a plateau means.

assignment.title: The plan you will actually follow
assignment.instructions:
This is the last piece of work in the course, and it is for you rather than for anybody else.
Part one. Write your own learning plan for the next six months, in six sections and
about 180 words: Where I am, The gap, Priority, Habit, Benchmark, What I expect to
go wrong.
Section 1 must use both the present perfect continuous and the past perfect continuous.
The gap must name WHEN it fails, precisely enough that somebody else could design the
practice from it without asking you a single question.
The priority must be one thing, and you must name what you are setting aside.
The habit must name a time and a place, not an amount.
The benchmark must be fixed, dated, and something you can repeat.
Part two. Write four sentences about your own progress using good at, a gap in,
working on and improve, each with the right preposition or none.
Part three. Give your plan to somebody else and ask them one question: from the gap
alone, what practice would you design? Write down what they say.
If it is not what you had in mind, the gap is not precise enough yet. Rewrite it.
Part four. Write one sentence to yourself for December, to be read when you open
this plan again.
